```{r setup}
library(scopusflow)
```

The Elsevier Scopus Search API bounds a retrieval in three ways. A weekly quota
limits how many requests you may make, a short-term rate limit caps how fast you
may make them, and the ordinary offset paging stops at the first 5000 records of
a query. This article shows how scopusflow works within those bounds to make a
large retrieval reproducible, efficient and resumable. The steps that contact
the API need a key and are not run here. Everything else runs offline.

## A query, built safely

Most queries combine a few terms under a field tag. `scopus_query()` assembles
them without the bracket and tag mistakes that arise when fragments are pasted
together by hand.

```{r}
q <- scopus_query("language learning", "effect size", .field = "TITLE-ABS-KEY")
q
```

The recognised field tags, and what each one searches, are listed by
`scopus_field_tags()`.

```{r}
scopus_field_tags()
```

## Describing the search as a plan

A plan records exactly what will be fetched, so it can be saved, reviewed and
re-run. Partitioning by year is the recommended way to stay under the
5000-record ceiling, since each year becomes its own cell.

```{r}
plan <- scopus_plan(q, years = 2010:2020, partition = "year")
plan
```

Each cell carries the query, the year, the view and the page size.

## Why page size is a quota decision

Scopus charges quota by the request. A page may hold up to 200 records under the
`STANDARD` view, or 25 under `COMPLETE`, so retrieving a thousand records in
pages of 200 costs five requests where pages of 25 would cost forty. For that
reason, `page_size` defaults to the largest page the view allows, as `rscopus`
also does. At any page size, every request is counted and the 5000-record
ceiling holds.

```{r}
scopus_plan(q, view = "STANDARD")$page_size[1]
scopus_plan(q, view = "COMPLETE")$page_size[1]
```

## Sizing before spending

Counting is cheap and does not download records, so it is worth doing first. A
workflow can read the parsed quota attached to the count and decide whether
enough quota remains to proceed.

```{r eval = FALSE}
n <- scopus_count(q, years = 2010:2020)
n
attr(n, "quota")
```

The quota is parsed from the response headers by `scopus_quota()`. To show its
shape without a network call, apply the function to a constructed response.

```{r}
resp <- httr2::response(
  status_code = 200,
  headers = list(
    `X-RateLimit-Limit`     = "20000",
    `X-RateLimit-Remaining` = "19987",
    `X-RateLimit-Reset`     = "1700000000"
  )
)
scopus_quota(resp)
```

## Fetching, with caching and resume

`scopus_fetch_plan()` runs each cell in turn. Given a cache directory, it writes
each cell to disk as it completes, so a run interrupted halfway, or stopped by
the quota, resumes from where it left off and never spends quota twice on the
same cell. The plan below keeps its cells in a directory of its own inside the
managed cache, the directory returned by `scopus_cache_dir()`.

```{r eval = FALSE}
records <- scopus_fetch_plan(
  plan,
  cache_dir = file.path(scopus_cache_dir(), "language-learning-effect-size"),
  resume = TRUE
)
records
```

A cache directory belongs to one plan. Cells are checkpointed by their position
in the plan and their year, so a second plan pointed at the same directory could
otherwise be paired with the first plan's checkpoints. Before loading a
checkpoint, `scopus_fetch_plan()` checks that the query, year, view, page size,
paging mode and record cap it was written under all match the cell being run,
and refetches with a warning when they do not. Give each plan its own directory
all the same.

A checkpoint holding more records than the current `max_results` asks for is
served trimmed to that cap, with the fuller set left on disk for a later, wider
request. A checkpoint that stopped at a smaller cap than is being asked for now
is a mismatch, refetched with a warning. One that ran to the end of its result
set is not a mismatch, however few records it holds, because there is nothing
further to fetch.

To force a fresh retrieval, empty the managed cache with `scopus_cache_clear()`,
which removes every plan's directory inside it. Both functions are shown below
but not run, so building the article leaves any existing cache intact.

```{r eval = FALSE}
scopus_cache_dir()    # where completed cells are written
scopus_cache_clear()  # remove them, so the next run re-fetches from scratch
```

The result of `scopus_fetch_plan()` is a `scopus_records` tibble, the same shape
returned by `scopus_fetch()` for a single query. Without a key, the bundled
`example_records` stands in for it. It holds 138 published journal articles in
that same schema and is included because Scopus records may not be
redistributed.

```{r}
head(example_records)
```

## Watching progress

Per-cell progress is silent by default. For a harvest that spans many years, it
is worth setting `verbose = TRUE`, which reports a line as each cell is fetched
or loaded from cache.

```{r eval = FALSE}
records <- scopus_fetch_plan(
  plan,
  cache_dir = file.path(scopus_cache_dir(), "language-learning-effect-size"),
  verbose = TRUE
)
```

## Combining separate retrievals

Results gathered in separate runs are combined with `scopus_combine()`, which
renumbers the records and can drop duplicates by Scopus identifier or DOI. This
is preferable to `rbind()`, which would leave duplicate entry numbers. Here, a
baseline retrieval that stopped at 2023 is merged with a later one covering the
whole period.

```{r}
baseline <- example_records[example_records$year <= 2023, ]
combined <- scopus_combine(baseline, example_records, dedupe = TRUE)
nrow(combined)
```

The 138 distinct articles come back as 149 rows. De-duplication needs an
identifier to match on, and these records carry no Scopus identifier, never
having come from Scopus. Matching therefore falls back to the DOI, and the
eleven articles without a DOI cannot be matched to their own copies. A live
Scopus harvest carries an identifier on every record, so the same call would
return 138.

## Writing the search up

A harvest is rarely the end of the work. A systematic review has to report the
search itself, in enough detail that a reader can repeat it, and the reporting
standard for that is PRISMA-S
([Rethlefsen et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13643-020-01542-z)).
`scopus_search_report()` assembles the search record from what the plan and the
harvest already carry.

A plan on its own can be reported before it is run, which is useful when a
protocol has to be registered in advance. The plan below describes a Scopus
search for the phrase the bundled corpus was drawn on. The corpus itself came
from OpenAlex's exact-phrase search for 'graphene supercapacitor' in titles and
abstracts, limited to journal articles, on 22 July 2026. A Scopus run of this
plan would return a different set of records. The query puts the two words in
quotation marks so that Scopus searches them as a phrase. Without the quotation
marks, Scopus would join the two words with AND, and in OpenAlex the unquoted
words match about a hundred times as many records.

```{r}
graphene <- scopus_plan('"graphene supercapacitor"', years = 2015:2024,
                        field = "TITLE-ABS-KEY", partition = "year")
report <- scopus_search_report(graphene)
report
```

Much of the record says 'unrecorded'. Nothing has been retrieved yet, so there
is nothing to state, and the record says so in words because a blank would be
read as a zero. Throughout, the record states only what the objects hold. It
never substitutes the current time for a retrieval that did not record one,
never gives a completeness figure for a harvest whose reported total is unknown,
and never counts duplicates unless a merge recorded removing them.

After a harvest, the record fills in. `scopus_fetch_plan()` attaches the plan,
the retrieval time, the version, the paging mode and the per-cell accounting,
and you never set any of them yourself. Here, the bundled corpus stands in for a
harvest, since Scopus records may not be redistributed. Those attributes are
therefore written out below to show what each one contributes. Their values are
illustrative, so the record they produce describes no search that was run. The
retrieval time and the version are set by hand. Each cell's reported total is
the number of bundled records in its year, a count from the OpenAlex search
that the Scopus API never gave.

```{r}
# Illustrative values, set by hand. No Scopus search was run.
records <- example_records
attr(records, "plan") <- graphene
attr(records, "retrieved_at") <- as.POSIXct("2026-07-22 09:15:00", tz = "UTC")
attr(records, "scopusflow_version") <- "0.3.0"
attr(records, "paging") <- "offset"
per_year <- as.integer(table(example_records$year))
attr(records, "cell_totals") <- tibble::tibble(
  cell = 1:10, date = as.character(2015:2024),
  n_records = per_year, reported_total = as.numeric(per_year)
)

report <- scopus_search_report(records)
report
```

The completeness lines show each cell against the number of records the API
reported for it, so a cell that came back short stays visible where a total
would have hidden it. The overall figure is given only because every cell
reported one. Drop any of those attributes and the corresponding line says so
instead.

A harvest run with `max_results` records its cap. The search record marks each
cell that stopped at the cap, and the completeness line says how much of the
shortfall the cap explains. The record's entry for PRISMA-S item 9 names the
cap, and the snippet that rebuilds the plan passes it.

The methods paragraph is the same record as prose, ready to paste into a
manuscript and edit.

```{r}
cat(format(report, style = "paragraph"))
```

Supplying a `file` writes the whole record as Markdown, including a runnable
snippet that rebuilds the plan. The file can serve as supplementary material.

```{r eval = FALSE}
scopus_search_report(records, file = "search-record.md")
```

Six of the sixteen PRISMA-S items are answered here from the objects, and a
seventh, de-duplication, would be too had these records been merged with
`scopus_combine()`. The rest, among them peer review of the strategy and grey
literature, are listed as yours to supply, because the objects do not record
them. Any other database the review searched is yours to name as well.

## Retrieving more than 5000 records

Under offset paging, a query matching more than 5000 records cannot be retrieved
in full from a single call. `scopus_fetch()` returns the first 5000 and warns.
One remedy is to split the search by year, or by any other facet, so that each
cell stays under the ceiling. `scopus_count()` tells you in advance whether a
split is needed. The other remedy is `scopus_fetch(cursor = TRUE)`, which
follows the API's cursor in place of an offset and retrieves the whole set in
one call. The records then arrive in deep-paging order. The *Analysing a
literature* article weighs a plan's cached, resumable cells against the cursor's
complete set in a single pass.

`scopus_fetch_plan(plan, cursor = TRUE)` combines the two remedies. It pages
every cell of a plan by cursor, so a single year that matches more than 5000
records is retrieved whole and keeps its checkpoint.

```{r eval = FALSE}
records <- scopus_fetch_plan(
  plan,
  cache_dir = file.path(scopus_cache_dir(), "language-learning-effect-size"),
  cursor = TRUE
)
```

Inside a plan, the warning for a cell that stops at the ceiling names
`scopus_fetch_plan(plan, cursor = TRUE)`, since the cell is already partitioned.
Plans page by offset unless given `cursor = TRUE`. A checkpoint records the mode
it was fetched under and serves only a harvest in the same mode, so switching
modes fetches each cell again. The Python twin's `fetch_plan()` pages by cursor
by default, and by offset when given `cursor=False`, the route pybliometrics
documents for keys without a Scopus subscription.

## Handling interruptions

Network and API problems are raised as typed conditions, all inheriting from
`scopus_error`, so a long retrieval can catch them and carry on.

```{r eval = FALSE}
result <- tryCatch(
  scopus_fetch_plan(
    plan,
    cache_dir = file.path(scopus_cache_dir(), "language-learning-effect-size")
  ),
  scopus_error_rate_limit = function(e) {
    message("Rate limited; the cached cells are safe. Try again later.")
    NULL
  }
)
```

Because each completed cell is cached, resuming after such a pause costs nothing
for the work already done.

Elsevier answers throttling and a spent weekly quota alike with HTTP 429.
Throttling is retried with back-off before any condition is raised. A spent
quota is not, since it resets only days later. It is raised as
`scopus_error_quota_exceeded`, a subclass of `scopus_error_rate_limit`, so the
handler above catches it too, and its message gives the time the quota resets.
